sources.citation: Lawrence Mykytiuk, "Archaeology Confirms 50 Real People in the Bible", Biblical Archaeology Review 40:2 (March/April 2014), with its web endnotes
Lawrence Mykytiuk, "Archaeology Confirms 3 More Bible People", Biblical Archaeology Review 43:3 (May/June 2017)
Wikipedia, the article on the find (CC BY-SA 4.0)

artifacts.name: Merneptah Stele
artifacts.summary: Pharaoh Merneptah's victory hymn, which lists among the peoples of Canaan he defeated "Israel", written with the sign for a people rather than a land: the earliest mention of Israel outside the Bible.

attests.name: Ashkelon
attests.how: "Ashkelon has been overcome", among the Canaanite towns Merneptah claims, just before Israel.

attests.name: Gezer
attests.how: "Gezer has been captured", in the same line.

artifacts.note: Names Israel as a people in Canaan by about 1208 BC. TIPNR has no record for Israel the people (only Jacob, Israel@Gen.25.26), so it is linked to nothing and shows in no chapter; it would show in a list of all finds. Should it be tied to a passage, such as Judges 1, or left unlinked?

artifacts.name: Deir Alla inscription
artifacts.script: Aramaic or a Canaanite dialect, in ink on plaster
artifacts.summary: A text painted on a plastered wall telling of a night vision of "Balaam son of Beor, a seer of the gods".

attests.name: Balaam
attests.how: Named with his father and his calling, as in Numbers 22:5, but written centuries after the Bible sets him: it shows a Balaam tradition in Transjordan, not that the inscription is of his time.

artifacts.name: Bubastite Portal
other_names: Shoshenq I's campaign relief at Karnak
artifacts.summary: Shoshenq I's record of his campaign into Canaan, with the names of the towns he took, among them Megiddo, Taanach, Beth-shean, Gibeon and Mahanaim. A fragment of his victory stele was also found at Megiddo.

attests.name: Shishak
attests.how: Shoshenq I is the Bible's Shishak, who invaded Judah in Rehoboam's fifth year.

attests.name: Megiddo
attests.how: In the list of towns Shoshenq took; his stele fragment was found at Megiddo itself.

attests.name: Taanach
attests.how: In the list of towns Shoshenq took.

attests.name: Beth-shean
attests.how: In the list of towns Shoshenq took.

attests.name: Gibeon
attests.how: In the list of towns Shoshenq took, in the hill country north of Jerusalem.

attests.name: Mahanaim
attests.how: In the list of towns Shoshenq took, east of the Jordan.

passages.how: Shishak's campaign. The surviving list names towns in Israel and the Negev rather than Jerusalem, which the Bible says paid him off.
The same campaign, with the fortified cities of Judah taken.

artifacts.name: Mesha Stele
artifacts.summary: King Mesha of Moab's account of throwing off Israel's rule after "Omri king of Israel" and his son had oppressed Moab, of taking Israelite towns such as Ataroth and Nebo, and of carrying off the vessels of Yahweh.

attests.name: Mesha
attests.how: "I am Mesha son of Chemosh-[yat], king of Moab, the Dibonite" (lines 1–2).

attests.name: Omri
attests.how: "Omri was king of Israel and oppressed Moab many days" (lines 4–5, 7).

attests.name: David
attests.how: Line 31 is read by many as "house of [D]avid", but one letter is damaged and the reading is disputed.

attests.name: Dibon
attests.how: Mesha calls himself "the Dibonite" and builds up Qarhoh, Dibon's citadel.

attests.name: Medeba
attests.how: "Omri had taken possession of the land of Medeba" (lines 7–8), which Mesha retook.

attests.name: Ataroth
attests.how: "The men of Gad had dwelt in the land of Ataroth from of old, and the king of Israel built Ataroth for them" (lines 10–11), as Numbers 32:34 has Gad build it.

attests.name: Nebo
attests.how: "Chemosh said to me, Go, take Nebo from Israel" (line 14).

attests.name: Jahaz
attests.how: The king of Israel had built Jahaz and stayed in it while he fought Mesha, who took it (lines 18–20).

attests.name: Aroer
attests.how: "I built Aroer, and I made the highway by the Arnon" (line 26).

attests.name: Bezer
attests.how: "I built Bezer, for it was in ruins" (line 27).

attests.name: Baal-meon
attests.how: "I built Baal-meon" (line 9), and later Beth-baal-meon (line 30).

attests.name: Kiriathaim
attests.how: "I built Kiriathaim" (line 10); Kerioth, where Chemosh had a shrine, follows in line 13.

passages.how: Moab's revolt against Israel, from Moab's side.

artifacts.name: Kurkh Monolith of Shalmaneser III
artifacts.summary: Shalmaneser III's account of the battle of Qarqar in 853 BC, where a coalition including Hadadezer of Damascus and "Ahab the Israelite", with 2,000 chariots, stood against him.

attests.name: Ahab
attests.how: "Ahab the Israelite" among the kings at Qarqar.

artifacts.note: Also names Hadadezer (Adad-idri) of Damascus, whom Mykytiuk counts; TIPNR's only Hadadezer is David's foe (2Sa.8.3), and the Bible calls Ahab's Damascene rival Ben-hadad, so he is not linked.

artifacts.name: Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III
artifacts.summary: A carved obelisk of the tribute brought to Shalmaneser III, with a panel of "Jehu of the house of Omri" (or his envoy) bowing before the king: the only picture of a king of Israel or Judah from his time.

attests.name: Jehu
attests.how: "The tribute of Jehu of the house of Omri" (Assyrian Bit-Humri, the name for Israel).

attests.name: Hazael
attests.how: Shalmaneser's wars with Hazael of Damascus.

artifacts.name: Tel Dan Stele
artifacts.summary: Fragments of an Aramean king's victory stele, most likely Hazael's, boasting of killing a king of Israel and a king of the "house of David": the first mention of David found outside the Bible.

attests.name: David
attests.how: "The house of David" (bytdwd), Judah's royal line, about 150 years after him.

passages.how: The king of Israel and king of the house of David it boasts of killing are usually restored as Joram son of Ahab and Ahaziah son of Joram, whom the Bible says Jehu killed. The names are restored and the claim differs from the Bible's.

artifacts.name: Melqart stele
artifacts.summary: A stele set up to the god Melqart by Bar-Hadad, king of Aram.

attests.name: Ben-hadad
attests.how: Mykytiuk reads the dedicator as Ben-hadad son of Hadadezer, king of Aram; the line naming his father is worn and read in several ways.

artifacts.name: Stele of Zakkur
artifacts.summary: King Zakkur of Hamath's thanks to his god for saving him from a siege by a coalition led by "Bar-Hadad son of Hazael, king of Aram".

attests.name: Ben-hadad
attests.how: "Bar-Hadad son of Hazael, king of Aram" (lines 4–5): name, father and title as in 2 Kings 13:3.

attests.name: Hazael
attests.how: Named as Bar-Hadad's father.

artifacts.name: Tell al-Rimah stela of Adad-nirari III
artifacts.summary: Adad-nirari III's record of tribute received in the west, from "Joash the Samarian" among others.

attests.name: Joash
attests.how: "Joash (Iu'asu) the Samarian", king of Israel.

artifacts.name: Seal of Shema, servant of Jeroboam
artifacts.summary: A jasper seal with a roaring lion, inscribed "Belonging to Shema, servant of Jeroboam".

attests.name: Jeroboam
attests.how: "Servant" was a royal official's title. Most date the seal to Jeroboam II; a few to Jeroboam I.

artifacts.name: Seals of Abiyaw and Shubnayaw, servants of Uzziah
artifacts.summary: Two seals of royal officials, each "servant of Uzziah".

attests.name: Uzziah
attests.how: Officials' seals naming the king they served.

artifacts.note: Neither seal has a find site or a museum I could confirm; check before shipping.

artifacts.name: Annals and summary inscriptions of Tiglath-pileser III
artifacts.summary: Tiglath-pileser III's records of his western campaigns: the tribute of Menahem of Samaria and Rezin of Damascus; the Israelites' overthrow of Pekah and his setting up Hoshea in his place; and the tribute of "Jehoahaz (Ahaz) of Judah", the first mention of Judah outside the Bible.

attests.name: Tiglath-pileser
attests.how: His own inscriptions. The Bible also calls him Pul, his name as king of Babylon.

attests.name: Menahem
attests.how: "Menahem of Samaria" among the tributaries (Calah annals).

attests.name: Pekah
attests.how: "They overthrew Pekah their king" (Summary Inscription 4, lines 15–17).

attests.name: Hoshea
attests.how: "I placed Hoshea as king over them" (Summary Inscription 4).

attests.name: Rezin
attests.how: Rezin (Rahianu) of Damascus, a tributary and then besieged.

attests.name: Ahaz
attests.how: "Jehoahaz of Judah" among the tributaries (Summary Inscription 7, K.3751): Ahaz's full name.

passages.how: Menahem pays the king of Assyria tribute.
Pekah overthrown and Hoshea made king; Galilee taken.
Ahaz's tribute, and Damascus taken and Rezin killed.

artifacts.name: Iran Stele of Tiglath-pileser III
artifacts.summary: A stele of Tiglath-pileser III listing kings of the west who paid him tribute.

attests.name: Menahem
attests.how: "Menahem of Samaria" among the tributaries.

attests.name: Rezin
attests.how: Rezin of Damascus among the tributaries.

attests.name: Tiglath-pileser
attests.how: His own stele.

passages.how: Menahem's tribute.

artifacts.name: Babylonian Chronicle of the Assyrian kings
artifacts.summary: A year-by-year chronicle that records Shalmaneser V "ravaged Samaria", Merodach-baladan's reign in Babylon, and Sennacherib's murder "by his son in a rebellion".

attests.name: Shalmaneser
attests.how: Shalmaneser V's accession and his ravaging of Samaria (Shamara'in).

attests.name: Merodach-baladan
attests.how: Marduk-apla-iddina II's kingship in Babylon.

attests.name: Sennacherib
attests.how: His reign and his death.

passages.how: Shalmaneser's siege of Samaria. The chronicle says he ravaged it; the Bible's "king of Assyria" who took it may be Shalmaneser or Sargon II.
Sennacherib killed by his son, and Esarhaddon king after him. The Bible names two sons.

artifacts.name: Annals of Sargon II
artifacts.summary: Sargon II's records from his palace, including his campaign against Ashdod in 711 BC and his claim to have taken Samaria and carried off 27,290 of its people. Fragments of a stele he set up at Ashdod were found there.

attests.name: So
attests.how: Mykytiuk takes So as Osorkon IV, named in Sargon's records as Shilkanni king of Egypt; the identification of So is disputed.

passages.how: Sargon's commander takes Ashdod: the one place the Bible names Sargon.
Samaria taken and its people deported. Sargon claims it; the Babylonian Chronicle credits Shalmaneser V.

artifacts.note: TIPNR files Sargon (Isa 20:1) under Sennacherib's record (Sennacherib@2Ki.18.13), so Sargon himself is not linked: linking would put Sargon's annals on every Sennacherib chapter. A Sargon record could be split out, as place_overrides.json splits places.

artifacts.name: Annals of Sennacherib
artifacts.museum: British Museum, London; Oriental Institute, Chicago; Israel Museum, Jerusalem
artifacts.summary: Sennacherib's account of his campaign of 701 BC: 46 walled cities of Judah taken, and Hezekiah shut up in Jerusalem "like a bird in a cage", paying 30 talents of gold and 800 of silver. He does not claim to have taken Jerusalem.

attests.name: Hezekiah
attests.how: "Hezekiah the Judahite", shut up in Jerusalem.

attests.name: Sennacherib
attests.how: His own annals.

attests.name: Jerusalem
attests.how: Hezekiah "I shut up like a caged bird in Jerusalem, his royal city".

attests.name: Ekron
attests.how: Ekron's nobles had handed their king Padi, loyal to Assyria, to Hezekiah; Sennacherib took the city and restored him.

attests.name: Ashkelon
attests.how: Sennacherib deposed Sidqa, king of Ashkelon, who had rebelled.

attests.name: Joppa
attests.how: Among the towns of Ashkelon's king that Sennacherib took.

attests.name: Eltekeh
attests.how: Where Sennacherib fought the Egyptian and Cushite army that came to Ekron's help.

passages.how: The fortified cities of Judah taken and Hezekiah's tribute; both give it as thirty talents of gold.
The siege of Jerusalem, which both say was not taken; the annals are silent on why Sennacherib withdrew.
The fortified cities of Judah taken.
Sennacherib's invasion of Judah.

artifacts.name: Lachish reliefs
artifacts.script: Assyrian reliefs, with an Akkadian caption
artifacts.summary: Carved panels from Sennacherib's palace showing his siege and capture of Lachish in 701 BC: siege ramps, the city's defenders, and its people led away, with the king receiving the spoil.

attests.name: Sennacherib
attests.how: Shown enthroned before Lachish, with a caption naming him.

attests.name: Lachish
attests.how: The caption has Sennacherib on his throne reviewing "the spoil of Lachish".

passages.how: Sennacherib at Lachish, where Hezekiah sends to him.
Sennacherib has left Lachish.
Sennacherib besieging Lachish with all his forces.

artifacts.name: Royal bulla of Hezekiah
artifacts.summary: A clay seal impression from a royal building, with a winged sun and the words "Belonging to Hezekiah [son of] Ahaz, king of Judah". Found in Eilat Mazar's excavations and published in 2015.

attests.name: Hezekiah
attests.how: His own seal: name, father and title.

attests.name: Ahaz
attests.how: Named as Hezekiah's father.

artifacts.name: Siloam inscription
artifacts.summary: Carved in the rock tunnel that brings the Gihon spring's water into the city, telling how two teams cut toward each other until "the stonecutters struck, each to meet his fellow, axe against axe".

passages.how: Hezekiah's pool and conduit bringing water into the city. The inscription names no king; the tunnel is dated to his time.
Hezekiah stops the upper outlet of the Gihon and brings the water down to the west side of the City of David.

artifacts.name: Broad Wall
artifacts.summary: A city wall about 7 m thick, found by Nahman Avigad, built over houses on the western hill as Jerusalem grew in Hezekiah's time.

passages.how: Houses torn down to fortify the wall.
"The Broad Wall" repaired in Nehemiah's day, usually taken to be this wall.

artifacts.name: Boundary stone of Merodach-baladan II
artifacts.summary: A boundary stone (kudurru) recording Marduk-apla-iddina II's grant of land to an official, with the king shown standing before him.

attests.name: Merodach-baladan
attests.how: Marduk-apla-iddina II, king of Babylon, shown and named.

passages.how: His envoys to Hezekiah, of whom the stone says nothing; it attests the king.

artifacts.note: I could not confirm its Wikipedia page; the museum number is usually given as VA 2663.

artifacts.name: Letter to Esarhaddon naming Arda-Mullissi
artifacts.summary: A letter warning of a plot, naming Sennacherib's son Arda-Mullissi as the one behind it: the evidence Simo Parpola used to identify Sennacherib's murderer.

attests.name: Adrammelech
attests.how: Arda-Mullissi, Sennacherib's son, as the Bible's Adrammelech.

passages.how: Sennacherib murdered by his son Adrammelech.

artifacts.note: Mykytiuk's 2017 article is the source for Adrammelech; check the letter's museum number and find site against it.

artifacts.name: Prism of Esarhaddon (Nineveh B)
artifacts.summary: Esarhaddon's list of the 22 kings of the west who sent materials for his palace, among them "Manasseh king of Judah". Ashurbanipal's Cylinder C names him again.

attests.name: Manasseh
attests.how: "Manasseh king of Judah" among Esarhaddon's vassals.

attests.name: Esarhaddon
attests.how: His own prism.

passages.how: Manasseh as a vassal of Assyria. The prism does not tell of his being taken to Babylon.

artifacts.note: Museum not confirmed.

artifacts.name: Shrine of Taharqa
artifacts.summary: A sandstone shrine from the temple of Amun at Kawa, carved with Taharqa, the Kushite pharaoh of Egypt, making offerings to the god.

attests.name: Tirhakah
attests.how: Taharqa is the Bible's Tirhakah, "king of Cush".

artifacts.note: Mykytiuk cites Taharqa's inscriptions generally; this shrine is one of them, chosen because it can be seen.

artifacts.name: Bullae of Azariah son of Hilkiah and Gemariah son of Shaphan
artifacts.summary: Two of the many clay seal impressions found in Yigal Shiloh's excavations in the City of David, in a building burnt in the Babylonian destruction: "Belonging to Azariah son of Hilkiah" and "Belonging to Gemariah son of Shaphan".

attests.name: Hilkiah
attests.how: Father of Azariah: the high priest Hilkiah, whose son Azariah succeeded him (1 Chronicles 5:39).

attests.name: Azariah
attests.how: Azariah son of Hilkiah, high priest.

attests.name: Shaphan
attests.how: Father of Gemariah: Josiah's scribe Shaphan.

attests.name: Gemariah
attests.how: Gemariah son of Shaphan, the official in whose chamber Baruch read Jeremiah's scroll.

artifacts.note: Two separate bullae; kept as one find because they come from one deposit. Split them if you'd rather.

artifacts.name: Bulla of Jehucal son of Shelemiah
artifacts.summary: A clay seal impression found by Eilat Mazar: "Belonging to Jehucal son of Shelemiah son of Shobi".

attests.name: Jehucal
attests.how: Jehucal son of Shelemiah, the official Zedekiah sent to Jeremiah.

attests.name: Shelemiah
attests.how: Named as Jehucal's father.

passages.how: Jucal son of Shelemiah and Gedaliah son of Pashhur, who heard Jeremiah's words: the two bullae found nearby name both.

artifacts.name: Bulla of Gedaliah son of Pashhur
artifacts.summary: A clay seal impression found by Eilat Mazar a few metres from Jehucal's: "Belonging to Gedaliah son of Pashhur".

attests.name: Gedaliah
attests.how: Gedaliah son of Pashhur, one of the officials who had Jeremiah thrown into the cistern.

attests.name: Pashhur
attests.how: Named as Gedaliah's father.

passages.how: Gedaliah son of Pashhur among the officials.

artifacts.name: Babylonian Chronicle of Nebuchadnezzar's early years
artifacts.summary: A chronicle of Nebuchadnezzar's first years: his defeat of the Egyptian army at Carchemish in 605 BC, and his taking "the city of Judah" on the second of Adar (16 March) 597 BC, seizing its king and appointing "a king of his own choice".

attests.name: Nebuchadnezzar
attests.how: Nebuchadnezzar II's campaigns, year by year.

attests.name: Jerusalem
attests.how: In his seventh year Nebuchadnezzar "encamped against the city of Judah" and took it on the second of Adar, 597 BC.

passages.how: Jerusalem besieged and taken in 597 BC, its king taken, and Zedekiah made king in his place.
Jehoiachin brought to Babylon and Zedekiah made king.
The Egyptian army defeated at Carchemish in Nebuchadnezzar's first year.

artifacts.name: Nebo-Sarsekim Tablet
artifacts.summary: A receipt for gold given to a temple by "Nabu-sharrussu-ukin, the chief eunuch", dated in Nebuchadnezzar's tenth year. Read by Michael Jursa in 2007.

attests.name: Nebu-sar-sekim
attests.how: The same name and the same title, the Rab-saris (chief eunuch), eight years before the Bible has him at Jerusalem's fall.

passages.how: Nebo-Sarsekim among the Babylonian officials in the middle gate.

artifacts.name: Prism of Nebuchadnezzar II
artifacts.summary: A list of Nebuchadnezzar's court officials, among them Nabuzeriddinam the chief cook and Nergal-sharezer the Simmagir.

attests.name: Nebuzaradan
attests.how: Nabuzeriddinam, chief cook: the Bible's Nebuzaradan, "captain of the guard" (literally chief cook).

attests.name: Nergal-sar-ezer
attests.how: Nergal-sharezer the Simmagir: the official of Samgar in Jeremiah 39:3.

attests.name: Nebuchadnezzar
attests.how: His own prism.

passages.how: Nergal-sharezer among the officials in the middle gate.
Nebuzaradan burns Jerusalem and the temple and carries its people away.

artifacts.name: Jehoiachin's ration tablets
artifacts.summary: Palace records of oil rations issued to captives in Babylon, among them "Ya'ukin, king of the land of Judah" and his five sons.

attests.name: Jehoiachin
attests.how: "Ya'ukin king of Judah", a captive in Babylon, with his sons.

passages.how: Jehoiachin a captive in Babylon, given his allowance by the king.
The same.

artifacts.name: Ishtar Gate
artifacts.summary: The blue-glazed brick gate of Babylon, with its dedication by Nebuchadnezzar II, excavated by Robert Koldewey.

attests.name: Nebuchadnezzar
attests.how: His dedication inscription, naming himself as its builder.

passages.how: "Is this not great Babylon, which I have built?" (4:30 in English Bibles): his building works, which his inscriptions boast of.

artifacts.name: Lachish letters
artifacts.museum: British Museum, London; Israel Museum, Jerusalem
artifacts.summary: Letters from an officer at an outpost to his commander at Lachish as the Babylonians advanced; one says they are watching for Lachish's fire signals "for we cannot see Azekah".

attests.name: Lachish
attests.how: Letter 4 watches for "the signals of Lachish".

attests.name: Azekah
attests.how: Letter 4: "we cannot see Azekah".

passages.how: Lachish and Azekah, the last fortified cities of Judah left standing.

artifacts.name: Ketef Hinnom scrolls
artifacts.summary: Two tiny silver amulets from a burial cave, found by Gabriel Barkay, inscribed with the priestly blessing: the oldest known text of any passage of the Bible.

passages.how: "Yahweh bless you and keep you; Yahweh make his face shine upon you …", in a shorter form.

artifacts.name: Nabonidus Cylinder from Ur
artifacts.summary: Nabonidus's account of restoring the temple tower at Ur, ending with a prayer for "Belshazzar, my firstborn son".

attests.name: Belshazzar
attests.how: Bel-sharra-usur, Nabonidus's eldest son. Other Babylonian texts show him ruling Babylon while his father was away at Tema.

passages.how: Daniel made "third ruler in the kingdom": third after Nabonidus and Belshazzar, if Belshazzar ruled for his father.

artifacts.name: Nabonidus Chronicle
artifacts.summary: A chronicle of Nabonidus's reign: his years at Tema with "the crown prince" left in Babylon, and the fall of Babylon to Cyrus's army in October 539 BC "without battle".

attests.name: Cyrus
attests.how: Cyrus's taking of Babylon.

attests.name: Belshazzar
attests.how: "The crown prince" in Babylon, not named here; the Ur cylinder names Nabonidus's eldest son.

passages.how: Babylon falls that night. The chronicle tells of its fall to Cyrus, not of Belshazzar's death.

artifacts.name: Cyrus Cylinder
artifacts.summary: Cyrus's proclamation on taking Babylon, telling how he returned the gods of conquered cities to their sanctuaries and "gathered all their people and returned them to their homes".

attests.name: Cyrus
attests.how: "I am Cyrus, king of the world, great king …".

attests.name: Babylon
attests.how: Cyrus tells of entering Babylon without a battle and of Marduk choosing him.

passages.how: Cyrus's decree letting the exiles return to rebuild the temple. The cylinder shows the same policy toward Babylonia's cities; it does not name Judah.
The same decree.

artifacts.name: Behistun inscription
artifacts.summary: Darius I's account, carved high on a cliff in three languages, of how he took the throne and put down the revolts against him; the key to reading cuneiform.

attests.name: Darius
attests.how: Darius I, in whose reign the second temple was finished.

artifacts.name: Tablet naming Tattenai, governor of Beyond the River
artifacts.summary: A promissory note dated in Darius I's twentieth year, witnessed by a servant of "Tattannu, governor of Across-the-River".

attests.name: Tattenai
attests.how: The same name and office as the governor who questioned the rebuilding of the temple.

passages.how: Tattenai, governor Beyond the River, writes to Darius about the rebuilding.

artifacts.note: Museum and number not confirmed.

artifacts.name: Gate of All Nations, Persepolis
artifacts.summary: The great gateway of Persepolis, with Xerxes' inscription: "I am Xerxes, the great king, king of kings … this Gate of All Nations I built".

attests.name: Ahasuerus
attests.how: Xerxes I (Old Persian Xšayāršā, Hebrew Ahasuerus).

artifacts.note: TIPNR's Ahasuerus@Ezr.4.6 is Esther's Ahasuerus too: it names his 29 words in Esther.

artifacts.name: Elephantine petition to Bagohi
artifacts.summary: A letter from the Jewish garrison at Elephantine asking the governor of Judah to help rebuild their temple. It says they had also written to "Johanan the high priest" in Jerusalem and to "Delaiah and Shelemiah, the sons of Sanballat, governor of Samaria", and is dated in Darius II's seventeenth year.

attests.name: Sanballat
attests.how: "Sanballat, governor of Samaria", whose sons now act for him.

attests.name: Johanan
attests.how: "Johanan the high priest", as in Nehemiah 12:22–23. TIPNR's record also holds the Jonathan of 12:11.

attests.name: Darius
attests.how: Dated by Darius II's reign. Nehemiah 12:22's "Darius the Persian" is usually taken as Darius II, though some take him as Darius III.

attests.name: Jerusalem
attests.how: They had written to "Johanan the high priest and his colleagues the priests who are in Jerusalem".

attests.name: Samaria
attests.how: "Sanballat, governor of Samaria".

passages.how: The high priests down to Johanan in the reign of Darius the Persian.

artifacts.name: Great Isaiah Scroll
artifacts.museum: Israel Museum, Jerusalem (Shrine of the Book)
artifacts.summary: The whole book of Isaiah on 17 sheets of parchment, about a thousand years older than the oldest complete Masoretic manuscripts, and very close to them in wording.

passages.how: A copy of the text itself, every chapter.

artifacts.name: Wine jar of Herod the Great
artifacts.script: Latin, in ink on a jar
artifacts.summary: An amphora of Italian wine from Masada addressed "to Herod, king of Judea".

attests.name: Herod
attests.how: Herod the Great, "king of Judea", as in Matthew 2:1 and Luke 1:5.

artifacts.note: No Wikipedia page of its own and no museum confirmed. Herod is also well attested in Josephus and on his coins; you may prefer a better-known find.

artifacts.name: Temple Warning inscription
artifacts.summary: A stone from the barrier around Herod's temple courts: "No foreigner is to enter within the balustrade … whoever is caught will have himself to blame for the death that follows".

passages.how: Paul accused of bringing Greeks into the temple and defiling it.
"The dividing wall of hostility", perhaps an allusion to the barrier.

artifacts.name: Pool of Bethesda

found.site: Near the Church of St Anne, Jerusalem

artifacts.summary: Twin pools by the Sheep Gate, divided by a central wall, so that colonnades on four sides and across the middle give five porches.

passages.how: A pool by the Sheep Gate called Bethesda, with five porches.

artifacts.name: Pool of Siloam
artifacts.summary: The stepped pool of the Second Temple period at the end of Hezekiah's Tunnel, uncovered during sewer works in 2004.

passages.how: "Go, wash in the pool of Siloam".

artifacts.note: TIPNR's Siloam is a form of the Shelah record (Shelah@Neh.2.14); John 9:7 is linked as a passage so the record's choice doesn't matter.

artifacts.name: Caiaphas ossuary
artifacts.summary: An ornate bone box from a family tomb inscribed "Joseph son of Caiaphas", Caiaphas being the family name Josephus gives the high priest Joseph.

attests.name: Caiaphas
attests.how: Josephus names the high priest Joseph called Caiaphas. Most accept the identification; some doubt the reading of the name or that it is his.

artifacts.name: Pilate Stone
artifacts.summary: A dedication stone from a building Pilate put up for Tiberius at Caesarea, naming "[Pon]tius Pilatus, [Praef]ectus of Judea".

attests.name: Pilate
attests.how: Pontius Pilate, Rome's prefect of Judea, in his own dedication.

attests.name: Tiberius
attests.how: The building it dedicates is a Tiberieum, in honour of the emperor Tiberius, the Caesar of Luke 3:1.

artifacts.name: Politarch inscription of Thessalonica
artifacts.summary: An inscription from a city gate listing Thessalonica's "politarchs", a title for city rulers once known only from Acts.

passages.how: Jason dragged before "the city authorities" (politarchs) of Thessalonica.

artifacts.name: Gallio inscription
artifacts.summary: A letter of the emperor Claudius to Delphi naming "Junius Gallio, my friend and proconsul" of Achaia. It dates his year in office to about AD 51–52, and with it Paul's stay in Corinth.

attests.name: Gallio
attests.how: Gallio, proconsul of Achaia.

passages.how: Paul brought before Gallio's tribunal at Corinth.

artifacts.name: Erastus inscription
artifacts.summary: A paving stone recording that "Erastus, in return for his aedileship, laid this pavement at his own expense".

attests.name: Erastus
attests.how: Romans 16:23 sends greetings from Erastus, "the city treasurer" of Corinth. An aedile is a city official, but whether the titles match, and the inscription's date, are disputed.

artifacts.note: TIPNR's Erastus@Act.19.22 gathers Acts 19:22, Romans 16:23 and 2 Timothy 4:20, which may be one man or more.

artifacts.name: Execration texts
artifacts.script: Egyptian hieratic, in ink on bowls and figurines
artifacts.summary: Curses on Egypt's enemies, written on pottery bowls and clay figurines that were then smashed. They name the rulers of towns in Canaan, among them, as most read it, Jerusalem, Ashkelon and Shechem: the earliest mentions of these cities.

attests.name: Jerusalem
attests.how: "Rushalimum" is generally read as Jerusalem, some nine hundred years before David took it.

attests.name: Shechem
attests.how: "Sekmem" is read as Shechem, a town of Abraham's and Jacob's stories.

attests.name: Ashkelon
attests.how: Ashkelon and its rulers are among those cursed.

artifacts.name: Annals of Thutmose III
other_names: Thutmose III's list of Canaanite towns at Karnak
artifacts.summary: Thutmose III's record of his first campaign, when he besieged a coalition of Canaanite kings in Megiddo, and the list of some 119 Canaanite towns he claims, carved on the temple walls at Karnak.

attests.name: Megiddo
attests.how: The battle and seven-month siege of Megiddo, the oldest battle recorded in detail.

attests.name: Taanach
attests.how: The army debated taking the road by Taanach before choosing the pass to Megiddo.

attests.name: Damascus
attests.how: In the list of towns at Karnak.

artifacts.name: Amarna letters
artifacts.museum: Vorderasiatisches Museum, Berlin; British Museum, London; Egyptian Museum, Cairo; and others
artifacts.summary: Some 380 diplomatic letters to the pharaohs Amenhotep III and Akhenaten, many from the kings of Canaan's city-states, who accuse one another of disloyalty and beg for troops against raiders they call the Habiru. Abdi-Heba of Jerusalem wrote six of them.

attests.name: Jerusalem
attests.how: Abdi-Heba writes as ruler of "Urusalim" (EA 285–290), complaining that the Habiru are taking the king's lands.

attests.name: Shechem
attests.how: Lab'ayu is said to have given "the land of Shakmu" to the Habiru (EA 289).

attests.name: Gezer
attests.how: Gezer's kings write to the pharaoh, and others accuse them.

attests.name: Lachish
attests.how: Lachish's kings write to the pharaoh; one letter was also found at Lachish.

attests.name: Megiddo
attests.how: Biridiya of Megiddo writes of Lab'ayu's attacks on his city.

attests.name: Hazor
attests.how: The king of Hazor writes to the pharaoh (EA 227–228); others say he has sided with the Habiru.

attests.name: Ashkelon
attests.how: Ashkelon's ruler writes promising loyalty and supplies.

attests.name: Gaza
attests.how: Gaza, Egypt's base in Canaan, is named in several letters.

attests.name: Tyre
attests.how: Abi-Milku of Tyre writes of his island city's want of water and wood.

attests.name: Sidon
attests.how: Zimrida of Sidon writes, and Tyre's king accuses him.

attests.name: Gebal
attests.how: Rib-Hadda of Byblos (Gubla, the Bible's Gebal) wrote more letters than anyone, some sixty.

attests.name: Acco
attests.how: The rulers of Akka write to the pharaoh.

attests.name: Damascus
attests.how: Damascus, in the land of Upe, is named in several letters.

passages.how: Canaan as many small cities each with its own king, Jerusalem, Gezer, Lachish, Megiddo and Hazor among them, as in the list of kings Joshua defeated; but a century or more apart on most datings.
The Habiru who trouble the kings of Jerusalem and the south have been linked to the Hebrews, but the word names an outcast class across the whole Near East, and the link is much disputed.

artifacts.name: Samaria ivories
artifacts.script: Carved ivory, with Phoenician letters as fitters' marks
artifacts.museum: Israel Museum, Jerusalem; Rockefeller Museum, Jerusalem
artifacts.summary: Hundreds of carved ivory plaques, once inlaid in furniture and walls, from the palace of the kings of Israel at Samaria.

attests.name: Samaria
attests.how: Found in the royal quarter of Samaria, Omri's capital.

passages.how: "The ivory house that he built": ivories from the palace Ahab's line ruled from, though they cannot be dated to Ahab himself.
"Beds of ivory" in Samaria, from the furniture Amos condemns.

artifacts.name: Pool of Gibeon and its jar handles
artifacts.summary: A round shaft cut 11 metres into the rock, with a spiral stair down to a tunnel to the water table, and dozens of wine-jar handles inscribed with the town's name.

attests.name: Gibeon
attests.how: The jar handles are inscribed "gb'n", Gibeon, which fixed the site at el-Jib.

passages.how: "The pool of Gibeon", where Joab's and Abner's men met; whether this is the pool the Bible means is debated.

artifacts.name: High place at Tel Dan
artifacts.summary: A large stone platform with a courtyard and a horned altar, the cult centre of Israel's northern kingdom at Dan.

passages.how: Jeroboam set a golden calf in Dan and made a house of high places there; the platform is taken as that sanctuary, rebuilt in later reigns.

artifacts.name: Royal Steward inscription
artifacts.script: Hebrew, cut in rock over a tomb door
artifacts.summary: The lintel of a rock-cut tomb in Silwan, across from the City of David: "This is [the tomb of ...]yahu who is over the house. There is no silver or gold here...; cursed be the man who opens this."

attests.name: Shebna
attests.how: The owner's name is broken off but for "-yahu"; some take him as Shebna (Shebanyahu), "who was over the house", but that is conjecture.

passages.how: Isaiah rebukes Shebna, "who is over the house", for hewing himself a tomb in the rock.

artifacts.name: Seal impression of King Ahaz

found.site: Unknown; in the Shlomo Moussaieff collection

artifacts.summary: A clay seal impression reading "Belonging to Ahaz son of Jotham, king of Judah", with a winged scarab.

attests.name: Ahaz
attests.how: "Ahaz son of Jotham, king of Judah", as 2 Kings 16:1; bought, not excavated, so where it came from is unknown.

attests.name: Jotham
attests.how: Named as Ahaz's father.

artifacts.name: Seal of Jezebel
artifacts.summary: A large seal of fine stone carved with Egyptian royal symbols and the letters "yzbl".

attests.name: Jezebel
attests.how: Its letters spell Jezebel, and its size and royal emblems suit a queen; the top is broken, and the name may not be hers.

artifacts.note: Avigad published the seal in 1964; Marjo Korpel argued for Jezebel in 2007. Its museum is unconfirmed.

artifacts.name: Isaiah bulla
artifacts.summary: A clay seal impression found a few metres from Hezekiah's, reading "Belonging to Isaiah nvy[...]".

attests.name: Isaiah
attests.how: Found beside Hezekiah's seal; if the broken word is "nvy[']", it reads "Isaiah the prophet", but the last letter is lost and nvy may be a place or a name.

artifacts.name: Bulla of Nathan-melech

found.site: Givati Parking Lot, City of David, Jerusalem

artifacts.summary: A clay seal impression from a large public building destroyed in 586 BC, reading "Belonging to Nathan-melech, servant of the king".

attests.name: Nathan-melech
attests.how: A royal official of the right name and time, in Jerusalem; but the Bible gives him no father to match, only his chamber by the temple.

artifacts.name: Seal impression of Baalis's servant
artifacts.summary: A seal impression reading "Belonging to Milkom'or, servant of Ba'alyasha".

attests.name: Baalis
attests.how: Ba'alyasha is taken as Baalis, king of the Ammonites, who sent Ishmael to kill Gedaliah.

passages.how: "Baalis the king of the Ammonites".

artifacts.name: Vase of Amel-Marduk
artifacts.script: Akkadian cuneiform and Egyptian hieroglyphs, on alabaster
artifacts.summary: An alabaster vase inscribed "Palace of Amel-Marduk, king of Babylon, son of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon".

attests.name: Evil-merodach
attests.how: Amel-Marduk, Nebuchadnezzar's son and successor, is the Bible's Evil-merodach.

attests.name: Nebuchadnezzar
attests.how: Named as his father.

passages.how: Evil-merodach, in the year he began to reign, released Jehoiachin from prison.

artifacts.name: Silver bowl of Qaynu son of Geshem
artifacts.summary: A silver bowl dedicated to the goddess han-'Ilat by "Qaynu son of Gashmu, king of Qedar".

attests.name: Geshem
attests.how: Gashmu, king of the Arabs of Qedar, is taken as "Geshem the Arab" who mocked Nehemiah's wall; the bowl is his son's.

artifacts.note: No Wikipedia article on the bowl or on Geshem the Arab; Wikipedia's "Geshem" is the Hebrew word for rain.

artifacts.name: Coins of Herod Antipas
artifacts.summary: Bronze coins struck at Tiberias, the city Antipas founded on the Sea of Galilee, inscribed "Of Herod the tetrarch".

attests.name: Herod
attests.how: "Herod the tetrarch", as Matthew 14:1 and Luke 3:1 call him.

artifacts.name: Coins of Herod Archelaus
artifacts.summary: Small bronze coins inscribed "Of Herod the ethnarch", the title Archelaus held over Judea, Samaria and Idumea.

attests.name: Archelaus
attests.how: Herod's son who ruled Judea in his place, whom Joseph feared.

artifacts.name: Coins of Agrippa I
artifacts.summary: Bronze coins, the commonest with a canopy and three ears of barley, inscribed "Of King Agrippa".

attests.name: Herod
attests.how: Agrippa I, king over Judea, is the Herod of Acts 12 who killed James and imprisoned Peter.

artifacts.name: Coins and inscriptions of Aretas IV
artifacts.summary: Coins and dedications of "Aretas, king of the Nabataeans, who loves his people", whose kingdom ran from Petra to Damascus' borders.

attests.name: Aretas
attests.how: "Aretas the king", whose governor in Damascus watched the gates to seize Paul.

passages.how: Paul let down the wall of Damascus in a basket.

artifacts.name: Tribute penny
artifacts.summary: The common silver denarius of Tiberius, with his head and the words "Tiberius Caesar, son of the divine Augustus, Augustus".

attests.name: Tiberius
attests.how: The Caesar whose image and inscription the coin bears.

passages.how: "Whose image and inscription is this?" The denarius shown was most likely this coin, the one in use.

artifacts.name: Coins of Pontius Pilate
artifacts.summary: Small bronze coins struck in Judea in Tiberius's name, with pagan cult symbols, a ladle and an augur's staff, unlike earlier prefects' coins.

attests.name: Pilate
attests.how: Struck in the years he governed, though they name Tiberius and his mother, not Pilate.

artifacts.name: Lysanias inscription at Abila

found.site: Abila of Lysanias (Suq Wadi Barada), Syria

artifacts.summary: A dedication by a freedman of "Lysanias the tetrarch", for the safety of the emperors, made under Tiberius.

attests.name: Lysanias
attests.how: A Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene in Tiberius's time, as Luke 3:1; it shows Luke did not confuse him with the Lysanias killed in 36 BC.

attests.name: Abilene
attests.how: Found at Abila, Abilene's capital.

passages.how: "Lysanias the tetrarch of Abilene" in the fifteenth year of Tiberius.

artifacts.name: Lapis Venetus
artifacts.summary: The epitaph of Quintus Aemilius Secundus, an officer who "by order of Quirinius carried out the census of the city of Apamea".

attests.name: Quirinius
attests.how: Quirinius as governor of Syria taking a census, as Luke 2:2.

passages.how: A census under Quirinius in Syria, by AD 6; how it fits Luke's dating of the birth under Herod is long debated.

artifacts.note: No Wikipedia article on the stone. Its findspot is uncertain and its authenticity was once doubted; the link to Quirinius stands on its text.

artifacts.name: Sergius Paulus inscription
artifacts.summary: A boundary stone of the Tiber's banks naming among its curators "Lucius Sergius Paullus", under Claudius.

attests.name: Sergius Paulus
attests.how: A Lucius Sergius Paullus of the right time and rank; whether he went on to govern Cyprus is not shown.

artifacts.name: Theodotus inscription
artifacts.summary: The dedication of a synagogue in Jerusalem by Theodotus son of Vettenus, priest and synagogue ruler, "for the reading of the law and the teaching of the commandments", with a guest house for visitors from abroad.

passages.how: A synagogue for Greek-speaking Jews from abroad in Jerusalem; some think Vettenus a freed slave and this the Synagogue of the Freedmen.
A synagogue built for reading the law, with a ruler, as the Gospels describe.

artifacts.name: Ossuary of Yehohanan
artifacts.summary: The bone box of a crucified man named Yehohanan, his right heel still pierced by an iron nail with wood on it.

passages.how: Nails, as Thomas says, though here through the heel; the only crucified body yet found from the time.
A crucified man given to his family for burial in a tomb, as Jesus' body was to Joseph of Arimathea.

artifacts.name: Nash Papyrus
artifacts.summary: A single sheet with the Ten Commandments and the Shema, the oldest Hebrew Bible text known until the Dead Sea Scrolls.

passages.how: The Ten Commandments, mixing Exodus's wording and Deuteronomy's.
The Shema.

artifacts.name: Rylands Papyrus P52
artifacts.summary: A scrap of a codex of John's Gospel the size of a credit card, the oldest piece of the New Testament generally accepted.

passages.how: The front: the Jews tell Pilate they may not put anyone to death.
The back: "for this I was born ... to bear witness to the truth".

artifacts.name: Herodotus, Histories
artifacts.summary: The Greek history of the Persian wars and the peoples around them, which names several kings the Bible names, from Egyptian priests' and Persian sources.

attests.name: Sennacherib
attests.how: "Sanacharib, king of the Arabians and Assyrians" marched on Egypt (2.141).

attests.name: Neco
attests.how: Necos fought the Syrians at Magdolos and then took Kadytis (2.159).

attests.name: Hophra
attests.how: Apries, Necos's grandson, and his overthrow by Amasis (2.161–169).

attests.name: Cyrus
attests.how: Cyrus's rise, and his taking of Babylon by diverting the Euphrates (1.188–191).

attests.name: Darius
attests.how: Darius son of Hystaspes (3.88 and on).

attests.name: Ahasuerus
attests.how: Xerxes son of Darius, whose empire ran from India to Ethiopia (book 7).

attests.name: Artaxerxes
attests.how: "Darius son of Hystaspes, Xerxes son of Darius, and Artaxerxes son of Xerxes" (6.98).

passages.how: Sennacherib's army overrun in one night by mice that ate their bowstrings (2.141): a disaster to his army at night, but told at Pelusium in Egypt, not before Jerusalem.
Necos defeated "the Syrians" at Magdolos (2.159), usually taken as Megiddo, where Josiah fell.
Apries given into the hands of his enemies, killed by the Egyptians after Amasis's revolt.

artifacts.name: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War
artifacts.summary: The Athenian war history, which tells how the exiled Themistocles wrote to Artaxerxes, newly king after Xerxes.

attests.name: Artaxerxes
attests.how: "Artaxerxes son of Xerxes, who had lately come to the throne" (1.137).

artifacts.name: Menander of Ephesus, Tyrian annals
artifacts.script: Greek; known only from Josephus's quotations
artifacts.summary: A Greek history of Tyre drawn from its royal records, lost but quoted by Josephus, with a list of Tyre's kings and their reigns.

attests.name: Hiram
attests.how: Hirom king of Tyre, who built temples in Tyre and sent riddles to Solomon; known only at second hand.

attests.name: Ethbaal
attests.how: Ithobalus, priest of Astarte, who seized Tyre's throne: Jezebel's father, "Ethbaal king of the Sidonians".

attests.name: Tyre
attests.how: The history of Tyre's kings.

passages.how: Hiram's dealings with Solomon.

artifacts.name: Philo, On the Embassy to Gaius
artifacts.summary: The Alexandrian Jew Philo, writing within a decade of Pilate's rule, tells how Pilate hung gilded shields in Herod's palace in Jerusalem, and only took them down when Tiberius ordered it.

attests.name: Pilate
attests.how: Pilate, "one of the emperor's lieutenants, appointed governor of Judea", stubborn and harsh, fearing the Jews would report him to Tiberius.

attests.name: Tiberius
attests.how: Tiberius orders the shields moved to Caesarea.

passages.how: "If you let this man go, you are not Caesar's friend": a governor wary of being reported to Tiberius.

artifacts.name: Josephus on Jesus
artifacts.summary: A passage of Josephus's Jewish Antiquities on Jesus, "a wise man" and teacher whom Pilate condemned to the cross at the accusation of the leading men, and whose followers, the Christians, had not died out.

attests.name: Jesus
attests.how: Most scholars hold that Josephus wrote of Jesus here, but that a Christian copyist added lines such as "he was the Christ".

attests.name: Pilate
attests.how: "Pilate, at the accusation of the leading men among us, condemned him to the cross."

passages.how: Pilate condemns Jesus at the demand of the chief priests and rulers.

artifacts.name: Josephus on James
artifacts.summary: Josephus tells how in AD 62 the high priest Ananus, between two Roman governors, had "the brother of Jesus who was called Christ, whose name was James" and some others stoned.

attests.name: James
attests.how: "The brother of Jesus who was called Christ, whose name was James", as Galatians 1:19 calls him the Lord's brother.

attests.name: Jesus
attests.how: "Jesus who was called Christ", mentioned in passing; almost all scholars take the passage as Josephus's own.

attests.name: Festus
attests.how: Festus had died, and his successor Albinus was still on the road.

passages.how: "James the Lord's brother".

artifacts.name: Josephus on John the Baptist
artifacts.summary: Josephus says some Jews saw Herod Antipas's defeat by Aretas as God's punishment for killing "John, called the Baptist", a good man who called the Jews to righteousness and to baptism, whom Herod had imprisoned at Machaerus and put to death.

attests.name: John
attests.how: "John, called the Baptist", who baptised and drew crowds.

attests.name: Herod
attests.how: Herod the tetrarch had John killed, fearing his influence on the people.

attests.name: Herodias
attests.how: Herod had married Herodias, his brother's wife, which brought on the war with Aretas (18.110).

attests.name: Aretas
attests.how: Aretas, king of Petra, whose daughter Herod put away for Herodias, defeated Herod's army.

passages.how: Herod imprisons and executes John; Josephus gives a political reason, the Gospels John's rebuke over Herodias.

artifacts.name: Josephus, Jewish Antiquities
artifacts.summary: The Jewish history by Josephus, a priest and general in the revolt of AD 66, which tells of the rulers, high priests and rebels of the New Testament's time.

attests.name: Herod
attests.how: Herod the Great's reign fills books 14–17.

attests.name: Archelaus
attests.how: Archelaus succeeded his father in Judea as ethnarch, and was deposed for his cruelty in AD 6 (17.339–344).

attests.name: Philip
attests.how: Philip, tetrarch of Trachonitis and Batanea, who refounded Bethsaida (18.28, 18.106).

attests.name: Annas
attests.how: Ananus son of Seth, made high priest by Quirinius (18.26), whose five sons were high priests after him.

attests.name: Caiaphas
attests.how: "Joseph, who was called Caiaphas", made high priest by Valerius Gratus (18.35) and removed by Vitellius (18.95).

attests.name: Pilate
attests.how: Pilate's ten years as prefect: the standards, the aqueduct, and his recall after the Samaritan massacre (18.55–89).

attests.name: Quirinius
attests.how: Quirinius sent to Syria to take a census and assess Judea (18.1–2).

attests.name: Judas
attests.how: Judas the Galilean, who rose against the census (18.4–10).

attests.name: Theudas
attests.how: Theudas, a would-be prophet whose followers Fadus cut down (20.97–98); but Josephus sets him about AD 45, after Gamaliel's speech, so he may be another.

attests.name: Herod
attests.how: Agrippa I, struck down at Caesarea while the crowd hailed him as a god (19.343–350).

attests.name: Agrippa
attests.how: Agrippa II, his son, who appointed the high priests (book 20).

attests.name: Bernice
attests.how: Berenice, Agrippa II's sister, who lived with him (20.145).

attests.name: Felix
attests.how: Felix, procurator of Judea (20.137).

attests.name: Drusilla
attests.how: Drusilla, Agrippa I's daughter, left her husband to marry Felix (20.141–143).

attests.name: Festus
attests.how: Porcius Festus, who succeeded Felix (20.182).

attests.name: Ananias
attests.how: Ananias son of Nedebaeus, made high priest by Herod of Chalcis (20.103).

passages.how: Agrippa in royal robes at Caesarea, hailed as a god, struck down and dead within days.
Theudas and Judas the Galilean, though Josephus's Theudas comes later.
Felix with his wife Drusilla, a Jewess.

artifacts.name: Tacitus on Christ
artifacts.summary: The Roman historian Tacitus, telling how Nero blamed the Christians for the fire of Rome in AD 64, explains their name: "Christus, from whom the name had its origin, suffered the extreme penalty during the reign of Tiberius at the hands of one of our procurators, Pontius Pilatus."

attests.name: Jesus
attests.how: "Christus", executed under Tiberius by Pilate; the passage is accepted as Tacitus's own.

attests.name: Pilate
attests.how: "One of our procurators, Pontius Pilatus".

attests.name: Tiberius
attests.how: "During the reign of Tiberius".

passages.how: Jesus executed on Pilate's order.

artifacts.name: Suetonius on Chrestus
artifacts.summary: In his life of Claudius, Suetonius writes: "Since the Jews constantly made disturbances at the instigation of Chrestus, he expelled them from Rome."

attests.name: Claudius
attests.how: Claudius, who expelled the Jews from Rome.

attests.name: Jesus
attests.how: Many read "Chrestus" as a misspelling of Christus, the disturbances being over Christ among Rome's Jews; but Chrestus was a common name.

passages.how: Aquila and Priscilla had come from Italy "because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome".

artifacts.name: Pliny the Younger on the Christians
artifacts.summary: Pliny, governor of Bithynia, asks the emperor Trajan how to try the Christians, who meet before dawn on a fixed day to "sing a hymn to Christ as to a god" and bind themselves by oath not to steal or commit adultery.

attests.name: Jesus
attests.how: Christ worshipped as a god by Christians in Asia Minor some eighty years after his death; it tells of their worship, not of his life.

passages.how: Christians in Bithynia and Pontus, whom 1 Peter addresses.

artifacts.name: Letter of Mara bar Serapion
artifacts.summary: A Syrian Stoic's letter to his son, setting the death of "the wise king" of the Jews beside those of Socrates and Pythagoras: their killers were punished, and the wise men live on in their teaching.

attests.name: Jesus
attests.how: "The wise king" whom the Jews executed, after which their kingdom was taken away, is usually taken as Jesus, but he is not named.

artifacts.name: Babylonian Talmud on Yeshu
artifacts.summary: A tradition that "on the eve of Passover they hanged Yeshu", after a herald had gone out forty days before because he "practised sorcery and led Israel astray".

attests.name: Jesus
attests.how: Yeshu, hanged on the eve of Passover, is often taken as Jesus, but the tradition is late and some take it as another man.

passages.how: "It was the day of Preparation of the Passover" when Jesus was crucified.

artifacts.name: Ipuwer Papyrus
artifacts.date: copied c. 1250 BC; composed in the Middle Kingdom
artifacts.script: Egyptian hieratic, in ink on papyrus

found.site: Egypt; sold by Giovanni Anastasi to the Dutch government in 1828

artifacts.summary: A poem in which the sage Ipuwer laments Egypt overturned: the river is blood, the land dark, cattle moaning, the poor made rich and slaves wearing their masters' gold, and the dead buried everywhere. Some have read it as an Egyptian account of the plagues of the Exodus.

passages.how: "The river is blood". Most Egyptologists read the poem as a lament for civil chaos in a stock Middle Kingdom form, composed centuries before any date for the Exodus; it has Asiatics coming into Egypt, not leaving it, and the red river may be flood silt or a figure of speech.
"All animals, their hearts weep; cattle moan because of the state of the land."
Trees cut down and grain perished on every side, like the hail and the locusts; but the poem lays it to neglect and disorder, not to a stroke from heaven.
The land without light, as the darkness over Egypt.
Burials everywhere and wailing throughout the land, as on the night of the firstborn; the poem names no firstborn.
Gold, lapis lazuli, silver and turquoise hung on the necks of slave women, as Israel asked Egypt for silver and gold; in the poem it is the poor grown rich, not slaves departing.

artifacts.note: Included because it is often cited as confirming the plagues; every link is 'possible' and says why. Line numbers beyond 2.10 not given: check against Lichtheim or Enmarch before adding any.

artifacts.name: Habakkuk Commentary
artifacts.museum: Israel Museum, Jerusalem (Shrine of the Book)
artifacts.summary: Habakkuk's first two chapters, a few lines at a time, each followed by the community's reading of it as fulfilled in their own day: the Kittim (Romans), the Teacher of Righteousness and the Wicked Priest.

passages.how: A copy of the text, quoted in full piece by piece; it stops at the end of chapter 2.
"The righteous shall live by his faith", read of those who keep the law and are faithful to the Teacher of Righteousness; Paul reads the same verse in Romans 1:17 and Galatians 3:11.

artifacts.name: Samuel scroll from Cave 4
artifacts.summary: The largest biblical scroll from Cave 4, with parts of most chapters of 1 and 2 Samuel, often agreeing with the Septuagint and Chronicles against the Masoretic text.

passages.how: A copy of the text, in fragments: not every verse survives.
A paragraph missing from the Masoretic text: Nahash had been gouging out the right eyes of the Gadites and Reubenites, and seven thousand had fled to Jabesh-gilead. Josephus knew it too.
Goliath is "four cubits and a span" tall, about two metres, as in the Septuagint, where the Masoretic text has six cubits.

artifacts.name: Great Psalms Scroll
artifacts.summary: About fifty songs, some forty of them psalms of the Psalter, mostly from its later books and in an order of their own, mixed with others, among them Psalm 151 and a prose note crediting David with 4,050 compositions.

passages.how: Copies of many of these psalms, in another order and with gaps.
Psalm 145 is an acrostic, but the Masoretic text has no verse for the letter nun; the scroll has it: "God is faithful in his words, and gracious in all his deeds", as the Septuagint.

artifacts.name: Deuteronomy scroll 4QDeutʲ
artifacts.summary: Fragments of Deuteronomy and Exodus, notable for its reading of the Song of Moses.

passages.how: The Most High fixed the bounds of the peoples "according to the number of the sons of God", where the Masoretic text has "sons of Israel" and the Septuagint "angels of God".

artifacts.note: No Wikipedia article; its date is unverified. The 32:8 reading is standard (DJD XIV).

artifacts.name: Deuteronomy scroll 4QDeutᑫ
artifacts.summary: A small scroll that seems to have held only the Song of Moses (32:9–10 and 37–43 survive), with a longer ending than the Masoretic text.

passages.how: "Bow down to him, all you gods", a line missing from the Masoretic text; the Septuagint has it as "let all the angels of God worship him", which Hebrews 1:6 quotes.
Hebrews quotes the longer Song of Moses that the scroll shows existed in Hebrew.

artifacts.name: Jeremiah scroll 4QJerᵇ
artifacts.summary: A fragment of Jeremiah in the shorter form the Septuagint translates, showing that the Greek's shorter Jeremiah goes back to a Hebrew text.

passages.how: Lacks verses 10:6–8 and 10, and puts verse 9 in another place, as the Septuagint does.

artifacts.note: Date disputed: Tov dates it c. 200 BC, Wikipedia's Cave 4 list says Herodian. Check against DJD XV.

artifacts.name: Daniel scroll 4QDanᶜ
artifacts.summary: One of the oldest copies of Daniel, among eight from Qumran, written within a lifetime of the date critics give the book.

passages.how: A copy of the text, in fragments.

artifacts.name: Daniel scroll 1QDanᵃ
artifacts.script: Hebrew and Aramaic, in ink on parchment
artifacts.summary: Fragments of Daniel 1 and 2.

passages.how: The text turns from Hebrew to Aramaic at the same point as the Masoretic text, where the Chaldeans answer the king "in Aramaic"; 4QDanᵃ, ᵇ and ᵈ keep the switch too.

artifacts.name: Paleo-Hebrew Exodus scroll
artifacts.summary: Large parts of Exodus in the old Hebrew script, with the longer, harmonised text later kept by the Samaritan Pentateuch.

passages.how: A copy of the text, in fragments, with additions repeating earlier speeches as the Samaritan text does.

artifacts.note: Extent beyond 6:25–7:19 and the Samaritan-type expansions are from DJD IX, not checked against Wikipedia.

artifacts.name: Job targum from Cave 11
artifacts.summary: An Aramaic translation of Job, the oldest written targum known, which ends at Job 42:11.

passages.how: A translation of the text, in fragments, ending at 42:11.

artifacts.note: Extent 17:14–42:11 unverified against Wikipedia; whether to call it a targum is now debated.

artifacts.name: Testimonia
artifacts.summary: A single sheet stringing together passages about the figures the community awaited: a prophet like Moses, a star out of Jacob, and a faithful priest. Its scribe also copied the Community Rule.

passages.how: "I will raise up for them a prophet like you", quoted of an awaited prophet.
Balaam's "star out of Jacob", quoted of an awaited ruler.
Peter reads the prophet like Moses of Jesus: the same passage, awaited as a figure still to come.
"This is indeed the Prophet who is to come into the world": the same expectation.

artifacts.name: Florilegium
artifacts.summary: A reading of Nathan's promise to David and of Psalms 1 and 2 as foretelling the last days, when the "branch of David" would arise.

passages.how: "I will be his father and he shall be my son" read of the branch of David to come.
The nations raging against the Lord and his anointed, read of the last days.
Hebrews joins the same two passages, Psalm 2:7 and 2 Samuel 7:14, of God's son: a pairing already made at Qumran.

artifacts.name: Son of God text
artifacts.summary: A fragment of a vision of the last days: "He will be called son of God, and they will call him son of the Most High... his kingdom will be an everlasting kingdom."

passages.how: "He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High... of his kingdom there will be no end... he will be called the Son of God": the same titles, in nearly the same words. Whether the scroll's figure is a messiah or a usurping king such as Antiochus IV is debated.

artifacts.name: Messianic Apocalypse
artifacts.summary: "Heaven and earth will listen to his messiah" (or messiahs)... he will "heal the badly wounded, make the dead live, and proclaim good news to the poor".

passages.how: Jesus answers John with the same signs, the dead raised and good news preached to the poor, a pairing not in Isaiah 61 itself.
The same answer in Luke.
Draws on Isaiah's anointed one who brings good news to the poor.

artifacts.name: Melchizedek scroll
artifacts.date: composed c. 100 BC; copied c. 75–25 BC
artifacts.summary: Melchizedek as a heavenly deliverer who proclaims liberty at the last jubilee, atones, and judges Belial, read from Leviticus 25, Isaiah 61 and Isaiah 52:7.

passages.how: Melchizedek as more than a man, without beginning of days; Hebrews and the scroll each make him exalted, in different ways.
"How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news", quoted and expounded.

artifacts.name: Halakhic Letter
other_names: Some of the Works of the Law
artifacts.date: composed c. 150 BC; copies c. 75 BC–AD 50
artifacts.summary: A letter setting out where its writers differ from the Temple authorities on purity and sacrifice, urging the reader to study "the book of Moses and the books of the prophets and David".

passages.how: "The law of Moses and the prophets and the psalms": the same threefold naming of the scriptures, though the scroll's reading is partly restored.

artifacts.name: 7Q5
artifacts.summary: A scrap of Greek papyrus with about eighteen letters, some of them uncertain, published in 1962 as unidentified.

passages.how: José O'Callaghan proposed in 1972 that it is Mark 6:52–53, which would make it the oldest New Testament text; to fit, it needs a variant and an omission, and most scholars reject it.

artifacts.name: Nahal Hever Psalms scroll
artifacts.summary: Fragments of Psalms from a cave of the Bar Kokhba refugees, close to the Masoretic text.

passages.how: Where the Masoretic text has "like a lion, my hands and my feet", it reads a verb, "they dug" or "pierced", as the Septuagint's "they pierced"; the reading of the letters is disputed.

artifacts.note: Date and the k'rw reading unverified against Wikipedia; the reading is disputed in the literature, hence 'possible'.
